text:
The first thing to know about Harrow Hall is that it was never finished. For eleven years the building presented itself as a completed object: six stories of postwar brick on the northern edge of campus, home to the Department of Comparative Literature, and a ficus in the lobby that had been dying at a rate of roughly one leaf per week since the Ford administration. It was only in the fall of my ninth year, when a man from Facilities stood in the department lounge holding a core sample the way a doctor holds an X-ray, that we learned the truth. Somewhere between the architect's drawings and the ribbon-cutting, a waterproofing membrane—"the envelope," he called it, as though the building were a letter that had never been sealed—had simply been omitted.

"Omitted how?" asked Professor Lindqvist, who had occupied the corner office since before the Berlin Wall came down and regarded all change as a personal affront. Gerry—that was the Facilities man's name—explained that the contractor in 1962 had either run out of money or run out of interest. The brick had been laid directly against the block; for eleven years the building had been absorbing the weather like a sponge wearing a costume of a building. We were people who worked with texts, and so we understood immediately: we had been working inside an error. A typo with a ficus.

The first sign came in October, when the north wall of my office developed a stain shaped, depending on whom you asked, like the outline of France, like a woman's profile, or like nothing—a stain being just a stain, said Lindqvist, who was fighting his own war against metaphor. Then came the smell—"like a basement's idea of a basement," offered Priya, the new assistant professor, who was on the tenure track and therefore careful to find things charming. The stain grew. Books on the lower shelves warped into gentle parentheses.

The repairs began in November and were scheduled, according to a cheerful email from the Provost's office, to conclude by spring break. The email used the phrase "short-term disruption," which those of us who had survived the budget cuts of 2011 read aloud in the tone of a hostage video. They started with the east wing; within a week it was wrapped in white plastic sheeting, so that from the quad the building appeared to be undergoing a medical procedure, and the sound began.

The sound became the organizing fact of our lives. It was not a single sound; it was a curriculum of sounds. There was the jackhammer, operated from eight until four with a lunch break we came to think of as a cathedral hour. There was the shriek of brick being sawn at a pitch only dogs and assistant professors could fully register. And underneath it all there was the sound of the building being wet: a ticking, a seeping, a soft administrative dripping into the twelve galvanized buckets that now stood in the corridors like an honor guard. I taught "The Novel of Disillusionment" that semester, which the students found hilarious.

The crews were perfectly nice. That was the worst of it. The foreman, a broad, sunburned man named Ray, learned everyone's names within a week and apologized constantly. "Almost done with this stretch," he would say. "Then we'll be out of your hair." He said this every week for five months. I came to understand that Ray believed it, each time, the way I believe, each August, that this will be the year I learn Italian.

By December the department had developed the customs of a besieged city. Facilities emptied the buckets on Tuesdays, but between Tuesdays the senior faculty had informal jurisdiction, and you would come upon Lindqvist at eight in the morning, grimly pouring a bucket into the men's room sink, a man who had once debated Derrida now performing the labor of a bilge pump. Priya organized a rota of dehumidifier duty; the machines acquired names—Bertha, Loud Boy, The Dean—and someone taped a sign to Bertha that said SHE IS DOING HER BEST.

The health concerns began, as health concerns do, ambiguously. It was a cough at first, migrating through the department like a visiting scholar. Then headaches, and then it was Dr. Fenn's eyes, which watered through every faculty meeting. Priya, who was pregnant by then—she had announced it in the same meeting where we were told the timeline had been revised to "late summer"—asked for an air-quality assessment, and after six weeks two men came with instruments that beeped thoughtfully in the corridors. The report noted "moisture-related microbial activity consistent with building envelope failure" and concluded that conditions were "within acceptable parameters for occupancy pending remediation." "Pending remediation," Lindqvist read aloud. "We are pending. The whole department is pending."

Priya asked whether she could teach her spring seminar off-site, and was told that off-site space was "constrained," and so she taught in a respirator mask until her doctor wrote a letter, after which she taught from a coffee shop on Fourth Street, her students discussing Kafka in a room that smelled, she reported with real longing, of nothing but coffee.

I will not pretend we bore it well. In February—when the crew discovered that the east wing's problems were also the west wing's—the department came as close to open conflict as a department of comparative literature can come: a series of emails of escalating politeness, and a two-week period during which Lindqvist communicated with our chair, Margaret, exclusively through agenda items. Margaret bore it with the helpless decency of a middle manager. She wrote to the Provost, whose office expressed empathy and shared a link to a counseling resource. She wrote to Facilities. Gerry came and stood in the lounge and looked at the ceiling with genuine grief and told her that the building, and here he chose his words, "wanted to be wet."

"What does that mean?" Margaret asked.

"It means water has a memory," Gerry said, which was the most poetic sentence uttered in Harrow Hall that academic year, and I put it in my notes for the novel seminar.

What we did, mostly, was adapt, which is the quiet scandal of such situations—not the suffering but the speed with which suffering becomes décor. By March I no longer heard the jackhammer unless someone visited from another building and winced. I held office hours wearing a sweater and a scarf and, once, gloves, because the crew had opened the wall behind my bookcase to the February air and I could see, through the gap, a slice of the quad. One of my graduate students, in the acknowledgments of her final paper, thanked "the bucket by the window, for its constancy."

Spring break came and went. Late summer came and went. The plastic sheeting yellowed and was replaced, and the new sheeting yellowed too. Somewhere in there Priya had her baby, a daughter, and brought her by the department in October—one year, we realized, after Gerry had first stood among us with his core sample—and the baby slept through the jackhammering, having been conditioned to it in the womb, and we all stood around the stroller with a tenderness we had not expressed toward anything in a year, and nobody said the obvious thing: that the child had been born into a world that expected her to tolerate intolerable noise and had equipped her for it.

It ended the following April—eighteen months after the discovery, five timelines after the original. Ray shook everyone's hand, the sheeting came down, and the walls were whole and dry and painted a shade called Alabaster that nobody had chosen. The smell faded over the summer, or we stopped smelling it, which amounts, neurologically, to the same thing. The ficus continued to die at its steady rate, indifferent to envelopes.

What did we do then? We did what the building had done for eleven years, which was to go on, unpersuaded by our own history. Lindqvist retired that spring, and at his farewell party, held in the lounge beneath a wall we all privately checked for stains, he said that he had worked in five buildings at three universities and that every one of them had been failing in some way he had not been told about, and that he had concluded this was not a defect of buildings but the nature of them, and perhaps of everything, and then he asked whether there was more sherry. Priya got her tenure file together. Dr. Fenn's eyes cleared. Margaret stayed on as chair, having been unable to find anyone willing to take the job, which is how most chairs are made.

As for me, I kept my office. The stain was gone, painted over, but I knew its geography by heart, and some afternoons I found myself looking at the wall where France used to be, the way you glance at a photograph of a house you no longer live in. I had applied, during the worst of it, to a job at a university in Arizona, where the buildings were new and dry as toast, and had not been shortlisted, and had felt a relief I would not have admitted to the search committee. Because the truth is that we had become a department not of literature but of endurance, and there is a kind of grim membership in that, a lodge you do not leave easily.

On the first rainy day of the following autumn, I came in early and stood in the corridor and listened. The rain came down hard against the brick. The building took it and held it, the way a sealed envelope holds its letter. I waited for the ticking, the seeping, the first soft drop into galvanized steel. Nothing came. I stood there longer than I care to admit, almost disappointed, and then I went into my office and opened my window a crack, because the room was stuffy, and because old habits, like water, have a memory.
